item.title: 💗 A recruiter asks you for professional references. What happens next? 👀 Some co
item.description:
💗 A recruiter asks you for professional references. What happens next? 👀

Some companies contact former managers or colleagues before making a hiring decision.

They're usually trying to understand what it was like to work with you, confirm aspects of your experience and learn more about how you handled responsibilities.

🔜 So, how should you prepare?

• Choose relevant references.
Someone who worked closely with you and can speak about your actual contributions is more useful than someone with an impressive title who barely knows your work.

• Ask for permission first.
Make sure they're comfortable being contacted and that their contact details are up to date.

• Give them context.
Let them know which role you're interviewing for and what responsibilities it involves.

• Protect your current position.
If you're employed and don't want your current manager contacted, communicate that clearly to the recruiter.

And remember, reference checks aren't always the final step. Some companies conduct them earlier, while others don't require them at all.

A good reference isn't necessarily the most senior person you've worked with. It's someone who can genuinely speak about your experience.

item.title: 💗 Does an ATS automatically reject your resume? You've probably seen claims that
item.description:
💗 Does an ATS automatically reject your resume?

You've probably seen claims that most resumes get rejected by an Applicant Tracking System before a recruiter even reads them.

But that's not how every ATS works.

An ATS is primarily a tool companies use to collect, organize and manage applications.

Some systems support automated screening based on employer-defined criteria, while others also offer AI-assisted features.

And here's something worth knowing: there's no universal ATS score or magic resume template that guarantees you'll pass.

So, what can you actually do?

• Keep your resume formatting simple and readable.
• Use relevant keywords naturally when they reflect your experience.
• Make sure your qualifications are clearly described.
• Answer application questions accurately.
• Follow the employer's submission instructions.

Your goal shouldn't be to beat an algorithm. It should be to make your experience easy to evaluate.

item.title: 💗 Ambassador, Community Manager or Ecosystem Manager: what's the difference in W
item.description:
💗 Ambassador, Community Manager or Ecosystem Manager: what's the difference in Web3? 👀

These roles all involve working with people and communities, but they're not necessarily the same job.

1. Ambassador - Representing a project
Ambassadors help introduce projects to new audiences through content, events, education and community initiatives.

Some programs offer payment or rewards, while others are voluntary. Being an ambassador doesn't always mean being a formal employee.

2. Community Manager - Supporting the community
Community Managers help keep existing communities active, informed and supported.

They may manage Discord or Telegram groups, coordinate announcements, answer questions and share community feedback with internal teams.

3. Ecosystem Manager - Helping the ecosystem grow
Ecosystem Managers often work with founders, developers, partners and teams building within a blockchain ecosystem.

They may help projects access resources, connect with relevant partners or participate in grants and accelerator programs.

🔜 Which career path fits you?

If you enjoy creating content and representing projects, ambassador programs might be worth exploring.

If you prefer community engagement and building relationships with members, Community Management could be a good fit.

If you're interested in partnerships, supporting builders and helping projects grow, Ecosystem Management might be closer to your interests.

The responsibilities can overla and titles vary between companies.

item.title: 💗 Quick resume tip: Don't make recruiters guess what you actually did. Compare t
item.description:
💗 Quick resume tip: Don't make recruiters guess what you actually did.

Compare these two descriptions:

❌ “Responsible for social media management.”

✅ “Planned and published content across X and LinkedIn, managed the content calendar and tracked engagement performance.”

The second example doesn't need impressive numbers or complicated language.

It simply gives someone a clearer picture of your responsibilities and experience.

Before your next application, check whether your resume describes what you actually did or just names the tasks you were responsible for.

item.title: 💗 Found a Web3 job that mentions “on-call responsibilities”? Here's what you sho
item.description:
💗 Found a Web3 job that mentions “on-call responsibilities”?

Here's what you should know 👀


Crypto markets run 24/7 and some teams need people available to respond when systems go down or security incidents occur.

That's why certain roles in infrastructure, security, DevOps and technical operations may include on-call duties.

But being on call doesn't necessarily mean working around the clock.

Many teams use rotations, where employees take turns being available outside regular working hours.

Before accepting an offer, it's worth asking:

• How often will I be on call?
• Will I need to respond during nights or weekends?
• How quickly am I expected to respond?
• Is there additional compensation or time off?
• What happens if an incident takes several hours to resolve?

These details can make a big difference to your actual working schedule.
